questions.question: Define final consumption expenditure by households (C) and by general government (G), give the composition of each, and explain the two items that are commonly but wrongly included in G.
questions.expected_answer: C is spending by households on goods and services that satisfy wants directly, and it is the largest component of domestic expenditure at roughly three-fifths of the total. It is composed of durable goods lasting three years or more such as vehicles and furniture, semi-durable goods such as clothing and tyres, non-durable goods such as food, fuel and medicine, and services such as rent, transport, education and medical care. G is current spending by national, provincial and local government on the goods and services used to deliver public services — public servants' salaries, stationery, fuel, medicines and electricity. Two items are wrongly included. Transfer payments such as social grants and bursaries are not part of G because government buys no good or service in exchange; the money is counted later, inside C, when the receiving household spends it, and counting it in both places would double count. Government capital spending — a new school, hospital or dam — is also excluded from G because it is investment and belongs in gross fixed capital formation.

questions.question: Define gross fixed capital formation, give its composition, distinguish gross from net investment with the figures used in the lesson, and explain why this component matters more for growth than the others.
questions.expected_answer: Gross fixed capital formation is expenditure on fixed capital — assets used repeatedly in production for more than a year. Its composition includes residential and non-residential buildings; construction works such as roads, rail, dams, ports and power stations; machinery and equipment; transport equipment; information and communication technology; and cultivated biological assets such as orchards and breeding livestock. Purchases of existing second-hand assets are excluded because no new asset comes into existence, and the change in inventories is capital formation but not fixed capital formation, so it is listed separately. Gross investment of R900 billion against consumption of fixed capital of R560 billion leaves net investment of R340 billion, and only that net amount adds new capacity; a country whose gross investment falls below its depreciation is consuming its own capital stock. Investment matters most because it raises productive capacity — the outward shift of the production possibility curve — raises labour productivity, creates employment both in building and in operating the asset, and lowers costs for every user of the resulting infrastructure. At R900 billion against GDP of R6 300 billion the ratio is 14,3 per cent, well below the roughly 30 per cent of GDP targeted in the National Development Plan.

questions.question: Using the figures from the lesson, show how gross value added, gross national expenditure, gross domestic product and gross national income are related, and explain in words what each conversion adjusts for.
questions.expected_answer: GNE is C of 3 900 plus G of 1 400 plus I of 900 plus the change in inventories of 50, giving R6 250 billion — the total spent by residents on final goods and services, printed by some sources as GDE. Adding exports of 1 900 and subtracting imports of 1 850 gives GDP at market prices of R6 300 billion; that adjustment corrects for the fact that residents buy some foreign output while foreigners buy some of ours, so a country can spend more than it produces and settle the gap through trade. GVA at basic prices is the production-side total of every producer's output minus intermediate consumption, before taxes on products; adding taxes on products of 700 and subtracting subsidies of 40 converts GVA of R5 640 billion into GDP of R6 300 billion, so that conversion is purely about the price at which output is valued. GNI converts domestic into national by adding primary income received from the rest of the world of 90 and subtracting primary income paid abroad of 240, giving R6 150 billion. South Africa's GNI sits structurally below its GDP because a substantial share of the profit generated inside the country is paid out as dividends and interest to owners abroad.
